items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that if [MATH: f(x,y)] is a function whose partial derivatives

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},]

Content:
exist and are continuous at a point [MATH: (x_0,y_0) \in \mathbb{R}^2,] then the gradient of [MATH: f] evaluated at [MATH: (x_0, y_0)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(x_0,y_0) = \dfrac{\partial f }{\partial x}(x_0, y_0) \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial f }{\partial y} (x_0, y_0)\,\mathbf{j} \, .]

Content:
Now suppose that the gradient vector exists at every point [MATH: (x,y)] contained within the set [MATH: U\subset \mathbb R^2.] Then, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f] is defined as the map
[MATH: (x,y) \longmapsto \nabla f(x,y), \qquad (x,y)\in U.]

Content:
As an example, consider the function [MATH: f(x,y)=x^2-y^2.] To find the gradient vector field of [MATH: f,] we proceed as follows.

Content:
First, we find the partial derivatives:
[MATH: (∂f)/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − y^{2}) = 2x; (∂f)/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − y^{2}) = − 2y]

Content:
Therefore, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= 2xi − 2yj.]

Content:
A sketch of this vector field is shown below.

items.title: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function

sections.normalized_html: Find the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = e^{2x-3y}.]
sections.readable_text: Find the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = e^{2x-3y}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The gradient vector field of a function [MATH: f] is given by [MATH: \nabla f.]

First, we find the partial derivatives: [MATH: f_{x}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(e^{2x − 3y}); = 2e^{2x − 3y}; f_{y}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(e^{2x − 3y}); = − 3e^{2x − 3y}]

Therefore, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is [MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = 2e^{2x − 3y}i − 3e^{2x − 3y}j.]
sections.readable_text:
The gradient vector field of a function [MATH: f] is given by [MATH: \nabla f.]

First, we find the partial derivatives:
[MATH: f_{x}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(e^{2x − 3y}); = 2e^{2x − 3y}; f_{y}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(e^{2x − 3y}); = − 3e^{2x − 3y}]

Therefore, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = 2e^{2x − 3y}i − 3e^{2x − 3y}j.]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Find the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = e^{2x-3y}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The gradient vector field of a function [MATH: f] is given by [MATH: \nabla f.]

First, we find the partial derivatives:
[MATH: f_{x}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(e^{2x − 3y}); = 2e^{2x − 3y}; f_{y}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(e^{2x − 3y}); = − 3e^{2x − 3y}]

Therefore, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = 2e^{2x − 3y}i − 3e^{2x − 3y}j.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The gradient vector field of a function [MATH: f] is given by [MATH: \nabla f.]

First, we find the partial derivatives: [MATH: f_{x}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(2y^{2} − x^{2}); = − 2x; f_{y}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(2y^{2} − x^{2}); = 4y]

So, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is [MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = − 2xi + 4yj.]

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points [MATH: (2,1),] [MATH: (-2,1),] and [MATH: (1,-1).]

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for [MATH: \nabla f.]

[MATH: ∇f(2, 1)|= − 2 ⋅ 2i + 4 ⋅ 1j = − 4i + 4j; ∇f(− 2, 1)|= − 2 ⋅ (− 2)i + 4 ⋅ 1j = 4i + 4j; ∇f(1, − 1)|= − 2 ⋅ 1i + 4 ⋅ (− 1)j = − 2i − 4j]

Now, we draw the vectors at their corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

To answer this question, we note the following:

Content:
- As we've seen, the gradient of [MATH: f] at a particular point [MATH: (x_0, y_0)] lies perpendicular to the level curve [MATH: f(x,y) = f(x_0, y_0).]
- Therefore, the gradient field vectors of [MATH: f] at an arbitrary point [MATH: (x,y)] lie perpendicular to its level curve at [MATH: (x,y).]
- Moreover, the vectors always point in the direction where [MATH: f(x,y)] is increasing.

Content:
Now, if we superimpose the level curves of [MATH: f] onto its vector field, we get a picture that looks as follows:

Notice that the field vectors are indeed perpendicular to the level curves.

sections.normalized_html:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

  • Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = -1,] we get [MATH: xy = -1,] which gives the hyperbola [MATH: y=-\dfrac 1x]

  • Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = 0,] we get [MATH: xy = 0,] that is, the lines [MATH: y=0] and [MATH: x=0]

  • Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = 1,] we get [MATH: xy =1,] that is, the hyperbola [MATH: y=\dfrac 1x]

  • Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = -2,] we get [MATH: xy =-2,] that is, the hyperbola [MATH: y=-\dfrac 2x]

  • [MATH: \cdots]

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

Note that [MATH: f(x,y)] increases as we move from left to right in the upper half-plane [MATH: y > 0,] and increases as we move from right-to-left in the lower half-plane [MATH: y < 0.]

Now, we recall the following facts:

  • The gradient field vectors of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

  • Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where [MATH: f(x,y)] increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

Therefore, the correct answer is III.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that if [MATH: f(x,y)] is a function whose partial derivatives

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},]

Content:
exist and are continuous at a point [MATH: (x_0,y_0) \in \mathbb{R}^2,] then the gradient of [MATH: f] evaluated at [MATH: (x_0, y_0)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(x_0,y_0) = \dfrac{\partial f }{\partial x}(x_0, y_0) \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial f }{\partial y} (x_0, y_0)\,\mathbf{j} \, .]

Content:
Now suppose that the gradient vector exists at every point [MATH: (x,y)] contained within the set [MATH: U\subset \mathbb R^2.] Then, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f] is defined as the map
[MATH: (x,y) \longmapsto \nabla f(x,y), \qquad (x,y)\in U.]

Content:
As an example, consider the function [MATH: f(x,y)=x^2-y^2.] To find the gradient vector field of [MATH: f,] we proceed as follows.

Content:
First, we find the partial derivatives:
[MATH: (∂f)/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − y^{2}) = 2x; (∂f)/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − y^{2}) = − 2y]

Content:
Therefore, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= 2xi − 2yj.]

Content:
A sketch of this vector field is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0e7a282fb1adfbe0252d58f466ec02be]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function

Example Prompt:
Find the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = e^{2x-3y}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The gradient vector field of a function [MATH: f] is given by [MATH: \nabla f.]

First, we find the partial derivatives:
[MATH: f_{x}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(e^{2x − 3y}); = 2e^{2x − 3y}; f_{y}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(e^{2x − 3y}); = − 3e^{2x − 3y}]

Therefore, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = 2e^{2x − 3y}i − 3e^{2x − 3y}j.]

Item 5 — Example: Sketching the Gradient Vector Field of a Function

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/ae5318226e1538c2b166e0591310b036]

Which of the above diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = 2y^2-x^2?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The gradient vector field of a function [MATH: f] is given by [MATH: \nabla f.]

First, we find the partial derivatives:
[MATH: f_{x}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(2y^{2} − x^{2}); = − 2x; f_{y}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(2y^{2} − x^{2}); = 4y]

So, the gradient vector field of [MATH: f(x,y)] is
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = − 2xi + 4yj.]

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points [MATH: (2,1),] [MATH: (-2,1),] and [MATH: (1,-1).]

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for [MATH: \nabla f.]

[MATH: ∇f(2, 1)|= − 2 ⋅ 2i + 4 ⋅ 1j = − 4i + 4j; ∇f(− 2, 1)|= − 2 ⋅ (− 2)i + 4 ⋅ 1j = 4i + 4j; ∇f(1, − 1)|= − 2 ⋅ 1i + 4 ⋅ (− 1)j = − 2i − 4j]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Relationship Between the Vector Field of a Function and Its Contour Plot

Content:
Consider the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = x^2+y,] shown below. How is this vector field related to the level curves of [MATH: f?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ff2e17c995e010574d56bde4cfbabc98]

Content:
To answer this question, we note the following:

Content:
- As we've seen, the gradient of [MATH: f] at a particular point [MATH: (x_0, y_0)] lies perpendicular to the level curve [MATH: f(x,y) = f(x_0, y_0).]
- Therefore, the gradient field vectors of [MATH: f] at an arbitrary point [MATH: (x,y)] lie perpendicular to its level curve at [MATH: (x,y).]
- Moreover, the vectors always point in the direction where [MATH: f(x,y)] is increasing.

Content:
Now, if we superimpose the level curves of [MATH: f] onto its vector field, we get a picture that looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c1048e1525fae0855c731ae5730941f1]

Content:
Notice that the field vectors are indeed perpendicular to the level curves.

Content:
We can use a similar idea to sketch the vector field of a function using its level curves. Let's see an example.

---

Item 9 — Example: Using the Relationship Between the Vector Field of a Function and Its Contour Plot

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/87979b85b4ea12aacf6bd158adc3fcb2]

Which of the above diagrams could be the gradient vector field of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = xy?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = -1,] we get [MATH: xy = -1,] which gives the hyperbola [MATH: y=-\dfrac 1x]
- Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = 0,] we get [MATH: xy = 0,] that is, the lines [MATH: y=0] and [MATH: x=0]
- Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = 1,] we get [MATH: xy =1,] that is, the hyperbola [MATH: y=\dfrac 1x]
- Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = -2,] we get [MATH: xy =-2,] that is, the hyperbola [MATH: y=-\dfrac 2x]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

[IMG: /graphics/5691898f126e352c214c8c48bb94c312]

Note that [MATH: f(x,y)] increases as we move from left to right in the upper half-plane [MATH: y > 0,] and increases as we move from right-to-left in the lower half-plane [MATH: y < 0.]

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] always lie perpendicular to its level curves.
- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where [MATH: f(x,y)] increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

[IMG: /graphics/54fea7979eb64dee5d535a276bd80c43]

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/55af8d7d2226cd79132c79e19bbce747]

Therefore, the correct answer is III.
